title: For developers, architects, product managers, business analysts and business users
summary: Anyone who owns a business need can develop, deploy and validate an AI-native application with PL. Business users and analysts drive discovery and acceptance, product managers scope and approve, architects and developers review design and build plans, and everyone validates the result in EAL.
takeaways: One chat serves every role; nobody needs to write code or a specification first.
Business roles own intent and acceptance; technical roles own design review and evolution.
AI-native means the application is generated, verified and run by the platform with roles, audit and a conversational runtime built in.

blocks.caption: Every role works in the same PL chat and validates in the same EAL runtime.

steps.label: Develop
steps.detail: Describe the need in the PL chat; PL discovers, proposes the Blueprint, writes requirements, design and build plan, and generates the application with tests. Business and technical roles approve at typed gates.

steps.label: Deploy
steps.detail: PL provisions the database schema and login, builds and starts the UI and API on reserved ports, registers the signed release with EAL and publishes roles to UME. Today this is Local Development; later environments are promoted by release manifest.

steps.label: Validate
steps.detail: Business Review shows browser evidence against requirements; you accept or reject. Then every role signs in to EAL with their own role and uses the application: chat, forms, approvals, full view.

blocks.caption: Develop, deploy, validate. Click a step for what each role does.

blocks.title: What AI-native means here
blocks.text: The application is produced from a typed Blueprint by the platform, carries its roles, audit and idempotency by construction, is used through a conversational runtime as well as a full UI, and is evolved through the same governed loop that created it.

plPrompts.label: Ask PL who it is for
plPrompts.prompt: Who is this platform for, and what can each role (business user, analyst, product manager, architect, developer, tester) do with it? Do not build anything.

title: The application development process, as a process diagram
prompt: Show me the app development process as a process diagram.
summary: Eight steps from a business problem to a running application. Four of them are your decisions; the rest are automated and evidenced by PL. Click any step for what happens, who decides and what it produces.
takeaways: Your decisions: approve the Blueprint, approve the work products, authorize Start build, accept the Business Review.
Everything between your decisions is automated and leaves evidence: manifests, tests, browser checks.
The same eight steps repeat for every later version of the application.

steps.label: Describe
steps.detail: Type the problem in plain words: who struggles, how the work happens today, what should improve, the fields and rules that matter. End with the request to generate the Discovery Blueprint. Three to eight sentences are enough.

steps.label: Discover
steps.detail: PL extracts the outcome, actors, journeys, data, rules and risks, then asks one question per turn with a measurable default you can accept or correct. It stops when enough dimensions are covered.

steps.label: Blueprint
steps.detail: The whole understanding in one card: entity, fields, states, roles, screens and a topology recommendation. Approve it or request a change. This is the cheapest moment to fix a misunderstanding.

steps.label: Requirements
steps.detail: Testable statements with validation rules and acceptance signals, each traced to the Blueprint. Approving starts the chain of downstream work products; later changes here cascade.

steps.label: Design and plan
steps.detail: Delivery Plan (which stages apply), Solution Design (components, contracts, data ownership) and Build Plan (exact files, migrations, tests). Each shown as what it decides plus a diff.
steps.artifact: Delivery Plan, Solution Design, Build Plan

steps.label: Build and verify
steps.detail: Scaffold, generate, provision the schema and login, migrate, build, start on reserved ports, typecheck, tests and browser qualification. PL only interrupts if it needs you.

steps.label: Review and release
steps.detail: The Business Review lists requirement-derived checks with evidence observed in a real browser. Accept to activate the release in EAL and publish roles to UME.

steps.label: Run and improve
steps.detail: Users sign in to EAL and work in chat or the full view. Change requests come back into the same project with impact analysis and a new version.

rows.label: Who decides
rows.value: Blueprint, Requirements and downstream approvals, Start build, and the Business Review are yours. Nothing passes those points without a typed decision.

rows.label: What is automated
rows.value: Understanding, discovery questions, drafting of every work product, generation, provisioning, building, testing, browser qualification, packaging, registration and role publication.

rows.label: What is recorded
rows.value: Every message, decision and result as events; every file with a SHA-256; every build with receipts; every release with an identity.

blocks.text: Open the cross-functional swimlane next to see the same process split by who does what.

plPrompts.label: Ask PL for the process
plPrompts.prompt: Show me the app development process on this platform as an ordered list of steps, marking which steps need my decision and what each step produces. Do not start execution.

title: Cross-functional delivery: who does what, in order
prompt: Show the app delivery process as a cross-functional swimlane diagram.
summary: Four lanes and thirteen steps. Business decides, architects and developers review, PL discovers, drafts, generates and verifies, and the runtime registers and serves the application. Click any box for the details of that step.
takeaways: Hand-offs alternate between a human decision and platform work; no lane skips another.
PL never enters the business lane: it proposes, you decide.
The runtime lane starts only after your acceptance in the Business Review.

sequence.label: Describe the need
sequence.detail: Create a project and describe the problem in plain words: people, current situation, desired improvement, fields, rules and examples. End with the request to generate the Discovery Blueprint.

sequence.label: Discover
sequence.detail: PL extracts actors, journeys, data, rules and risks and asks one question per turn with a measurable default. Option cards wait for the business answer; the composer is paused meanwhile.

sequence.label: Approve Blueprint
sequence.detail: Review the entity, fields, states, roles, screens and topology recommendation in one card. Approve, or request a change and approve the next version.

sequence.label: Confirm landscape
sequence.detail: Decide where the application runs. Local defaults place the UI, API and PostgreSQL schema on the platform host in one click; EKG can propose placements when it is online.

sequence.label: Requirements
sequence.detail: Testable statements, validation rules and acceptance signals, each traced to a Blueprint item.

sequence.label: Approve Requirements
sequence.detail: Approving starts the downstream chain. A later change to Requirements supersedes the Delivery Plan, Solution Design and Build Plan, which regenerate in order.

sequence.label: Plan, design, build plan
sequence.detail: Delivery Plan: which stages apply and the verification each needs. Solution Design: components, contracts, data ownership. Build Plan: exact files, migrations and tests.

sequence.label: Review design and plan
sequence.detail: The architect reviews components and data ownership; the developer reviews files and tests. Precise change requests go into Requirements so the cascade carries them.

sequence.label: Start build.
sequence.detail: Authorizes generation and local execution. Eligible only when all four work products are approved on the active revision and the session budget allows it.

sequence.label: Generate, provision, verify
sequence.detail: Scaffold, generate source, create the schema and a NOBYPASSRLS login, migrate, build, start on reserved ports, run typecheck, tests and browser qualification, record the release identity.

sequence.label: Register release, publish roles
sequence.detail: A signed release set is staged in the EAL registry; the application's roles are published to UME; a test identity is created for validation.

sequence.label: Accept in Business Review
sequence.detail: Read requirement-derived checks with browser evidence. Accept to activate; reject with a reason to return to Requirements.

sequence.label: Users work in EAL
sequence.detail: Users sign in with their roles, chat with registered tasks, fill confirmed forms, approve human tasks and open the full view. Every write is receipted and audited.

rows: Solution Design and Build Plan drafted

blocks.text: For an evolution of a released application the same lanes apply from Requirements onward, with an impact analysis step in the PL lane before regeneration.

plPrompts.label: Ask PL for the cross-functional view
plPrompts.prompt: Show the app delivery process on this platform as a cross-functional view: for each step, who acts (business user, architect or developer, the platform, the runtime) and what is handed over. Do not start execution.

title: The application lifecycle: create or migrate, release, operate, enhance, release again
summary: An AI-native application is created new or migrated from a legacy application, released through DEV, QA and PRD, operated, enhanced and released again. Today PL delivers the create-and-enhance loop in Local Development (DEV) and runs the app in EAL; QA and PRD promotion and legacy migration are designed and sequenced on the roadmap.
takeaways: Two entry paths: a new AI-native application, or a legacy application migrated into one.
Two ongoing loops: enhance and release again; migrate an AI-native application between environments by promoting its immutable release.
Available today: create, enhance, release to DEV, run in EAL. Planned: QA and PRD promotion, legacy migration.
statusNote: DEV today; QA and PRD promotion planned

steps.label: New idea or legacy app
steps.detail: A new AI-native application starts from a problem statement. A legacy application enters through modernization: repository and runtime discovery, a characterization baseline that is green before any change, and strangler increments. Modernization is planned; new applications are available today.

steps.label: Develop with PL
steps.detail: Discovery, Blueprint, Requirements, Delivery Plan, Solution Design, Build Plan, build and verification through the governed loop.

steps.label: Release to DEV
steps.detail: Local Development: schema and login provisioned, UI and API started on reserved ports, signed release registered in EAL, roles published to UME, Business Review accepted.

steps.label: Promote to QA
steps.detail: The immutable release manifest is promoted to a QA environment with its evidence; qualification runs there without rebuilding. Planned with the environment ladder.

steps.label: Promote to PRD
steps.detail: Production promotion under a customer-controlled installation with identity federation, secret references, backup and recovery drills. Planned with the deployment foundation.

steps.label: Operate
steps.detail: Users work in EAL; the Control Center monitors platform services; audit and activity are recorded; observations feed the next change.

blocks.caption: Create or migrate, then release. Click a step for details and status.

steps.label: Enhance
steps.detail: Describe the change in the application's project. PL classifies it as an evolution, shows the impact (fields, screens, rules, tests) and asks for approval.

steps.label: Regenerate
steps.detail: Downstream work products regenerate in order from canonical inputs; unchanged parts are byte-identical; migrations are additive and prior bytes preserved.
steps.artifact: Design and plan v2, new migration

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: Existing tests must pass; new tests cover the change; browser qualification repeats the business checks.

steps.label: Release to DEV
steps.detail: A new release directory and identity; activation replaces the previous release in EAL; the previous one is kept for rollback.

steps.label: Promote QA, PRD
steps.detail: Migrating an AI-native application between environments means promoting the same immutable release through the environment gates, never rebuilding it.

blocks.caption: Enhance and release again; migrate between environments by promotion.

plPrompts.prompt: What is the application lifecycle on this platform, from creating or migrating an application through release to DEV, QA and PRD, operation and enhancement? Say what is available today. Do not build anything.

title: Runtime architecture of an AI-native application
prompt: What is the AI-native app runtime architecture?
summary: Users reach the application through EAL. The application runs as its own UI and API processes with its own PostgreSQL schema and login. UME supplies identity and roles, the Integration plane supplies systems of record, Audit and EKG observe. No component shares credentials with another.
takeaways: EAL is the front door; the application never authenticates users itself.
Each application holds only its own database login; platform secrets never reach it.
Every request carries a signed authority that the API resolves live, so revocation takes effect immediately.

layers.title: AI-native application
items: Fastify API: role policy, idempotency receipts

blocks.caption: Runtime layers. Arrows of trust go down; evidence goes up.

sequence.label: Sign in
sequence.detail: The user signs in to EAL. EAL resolves the user's roles and application scopes from UME; the application never sees a password.

sequence.label: Launch with authority
sequence.detail: EAL opens the application's UI with a signed application authority reference bound to application, environment, tenant, subject and session.

sequence.label: Resolve authority
sequence.detail: On every request the generated API resolves the reference live against EAL and checks that the subject matches; expired or revoked authority is refused.

sequence.label: Read or write own schema
sequence.detail: The API uses its own restricted login. Integration-backed operations go through the Integration plane with pinned targets and receipts.

sequence.label: Audit + outbox
sequence.detail: Each write records an audit row and an outbox event in the same transaction; idempotency receipts prevent duplicates on retry.

sequence.label: Confirm to user
sequence.detail: EAL shows the result in chat or the full view and records the runtime task case.

blocks.caption: One request through the runtime. Click a box for details.

rows.label: Processes
rows.value: Two per application (UI, API) on reserved ports, started by the PL deployer and adopted by the managed runtime after restarts.

rows.label: Isolation
rows.value: Own schema, own NOBYPASSRLS login, allow-listed environment; row-level security policies in integration-backed apps.

rows.label: Observability today
rows.value: EAL activity and notifications, application audit tables, Control Center liveness for platform services. Application telemetry export is planned.

plPrompts.label: Ask PL for the runtime architecture
plPrompts.prompt: Describe the runtime architecture of an application built on this platform: how users reach it, how identity and authority work, where data lives and what is audited. Do not build anything.

title: Local development architecture on one workstation
prompt: What is the AI-native app local development architecture?
summary: Everything runs on the platform workstation on loopback: the PL chat UI and API, the training guide service, EAL, UME, EKG and Brain, the Control Center, and PostgreSQL with one database per service. Each generated application gets its own reserved ports and its own schema in the platformapps database.
takeaways: One workstation, loopback only; every service owns its database and never reads another's.
Local defaults place a new application in one click: UI port, API port, schema.
The same layout is what Central Development will run as independent deployables.

blocks.caption: Local development topology. Ports are the defaults on this workstation.

steps.label: Use Local defaults
steps.detail: The landscape nudge composes, resolves and confirms the placement for a new application in one click.

steps.label: Reserve ports
steps.detail: The deployer verifies and reserves a UI port and an API port; conflicts are resolved automatically and recorded in the release.

steps.label: Provision schema
steps.detail: A schema app_name and a NOBYPASSRLS login with a random password are created in the platformapps database; migrations run from the release.

steps.label: Start UI + API
steps.detail: Two processes with an allow-listed environment: the app's database URL, ports and EAL origins, nothing else.

steps.label: Register
steps.detail: Signed release set to the EAL registry on :3102; roles to UME on :3201.

blocks.caption: What Local defaults do. Click a step for details.

rows: File-based per service; never inherited by generated apps
PL managed runtime adopts and restarts application processes; Control Center for platform services
127.0.0.1 only; CORS allow-list for UI origins
One PostgreSQL instance; one database per service; one schema per application
PL API runs from dist; source changes need a rebuild and restart; the chat UI hot-reloads
